entry.evidence: While the results of O’Malley et al.8 apply on a global scale, the extent of remote triggering that is possible at any specific location is [...]

steps.action: The authors take as established their own earlier global finding that M>=6.0 events remotely trigger high-magnitude earthquakes within 3 days, up to 180 degrees away.
steps.quote: consistent with recent global observations of remotely triggered high magnitude earthquakes

steps.action: They pose the question of how susceptible each specific location along plate boundaries is to remote triggering, to be answered by a regional rather than fault-specific analysis.
steps.quote: the extent of remote triggering that is possible at any specific location is [...]

steps.action: They design a backward-looking binomial test, adopted from the earlier paper's Experiment 2, with a global baseline rate (0.501) of M>=5.0 events being preceded within 72 h by an M>=6.0 source event, computed from the declustered catalog.
steps.quote: Surprisingly, this ratio is almost exactly equal to 50%

steps.action: They assemble the declustered (Gardner-Knopoff) USGS M>=5.0 catalog for 1973-2016 and classify faulting type from matched Global CMT rakes.
steps.quote: When matchups are available, the strike, dip and rake of the primary focal plane are extracted.

steps.action: In Methods, they check catalog completeness at M5.0 against the magnitude-frequency distribution and the b-value-predicted counts.
steps.quote: we conclude that the global catalog is complete when using a threshold of M5.0

steps.action: They build the local method: within a ±2.85 degree box, compute mid p-values as the lower magnitude bound is raised from M5.0, then take the minimum p-value as susceptibility and its magnitude as the onset magnitude.
steps.quote: What results is a p-value curve as a function of the lower bound magnitude.

steps.action: They apply the method to a Peru subduction box (thrust events, onset M5.5, p<0.0001) and to an oceanic convergence box split by faulting type, where reverse and transform faults trigger and normal faults do not.
steps.quote: the triggering zone begins at M5.5 and has an associated p-value of < 0.0001

steps.action: They map susceptibility p-values and onset magnitudes along all digital plate boundaries, for all events and by focal mechanism (14% not susceptible, 86% susceptible, 19% p<0.05; 65% with onset below M6.0).
steps.quote: Plate boundary locations that do not exhibit this behavior (p-values ≥ 0.50; 14% of the locations) are shown in green

steps.action: They compare onset magnitudes with published corner magnitudes Mc: they match Boettcher and McGuire for Gofar/Discovery but not for Blanco Ridge, and fall consistently below Bird and Kagan's setting-wide estimates.
steps.quote: their estimates of MC are consistently greater than the onset magnitudes obtained here

steps.action: They bin onset magnitude by p-value (0-0.3) for each boundary type and fit lines, finding that onset magnitude decreases with susceptibility in the order subduction > convergent > transform > divergent; extrapolated to p=1, the lines approach Mc ranges.
steps.quote: the higher the susceptibility the lower the onset magnitude (Fig. 5)

steps.action: They test the projected onset magnitudes against synthetic time-randomized catalogs for the seven tectonic regimes; the observed values are extreme against 64 of 70 random results.
steps.quote: The observed data shown in Fig. 5 resulted in extreme values when compared with 64 of the 70 random results.

steps.action: They describe alternating highs and lows in susceptibility around individual plates, with a spacing that varies from plate to plate and crosses boundary types, and infer that an unknown physical mechanism is at work.
steps.quote: Closer inspection shows that the local spacing appears to vary from plate to plate (Fig. 6).

steps.action: They propose thin-plate resonance (plate normal modes) as a mechanism that modifies boundary conditions along plate edges.
steps.quote: A potential mechanism that we will consider is thin-plate resonance.

steps.action: They specify two checks: whether normal-mode patterns align with susceptibility highs, and whether global processes exist at the modes' natural frequencies.
steps.quote: We check for two aspects to be present

steps.action: They build an Abaqus finite element model of the Cocos plate (uniform ~11 km thickness, no slab, oceanic-crust properties from a Peru FEM, base pinned) and compute normal modes 4-30.
steps.quote: We constructed a finite element model (FEM) of the Cocos plate

steps.action: They compare mode shapes with the Cocos susceptibility highs (nodal lines align for modes 7, 9 and 24) and the modal frequencies (730.7-4270.8 μHz) with Earth's free-oscillation frequencies.
steps.quote: These values are within the frequency range of toroidal and spheroidal free oscillations of the earth

steps.action: They propose a specific triggering mechanism: one-sided negative (compressive) stress normal to the fault plane, generated by a normal mode, reduces the force binding the fault.
steps.quote: If a one-sided contraction occurs in the stress normal to the fault plane, then the force binding the fault plane together will be reduced.

steps.action: They compare the sign of perimeter stress for mode 24 with transform-fault p-values below 0.1: 22 of 30 coincide with negative horizontal stress (p=0.0053).
steps.quote: a tabulation shows that 22 of the 30 p-values < 0.10 are associated with negative horizontal stress

steps.action: They repeat the stress matchup on ten synthetic strike-slip catalogs (supplement); the observed matchup beats 9 of 10.
steps.quote: the observed data has a higher matchup rate (smaller p-value) than 9 of 10 random catalogs

steps.action: They report that the local results are consistent with the earlier paper's conclusion of systematic triggering from beyond the aftershock zone up to 180 degrees away (Supplementary Section 3).
steps.quote: is consistent with the results here

steps.action: Faced with onset magnitudes lower than published Mc, they keep the onset-Mc equivalence and invoke a physical process that lowers Mc by modifying fault boundary conditions.
steps.quote: We later suspected that the triggering magnitude was being lowered by a physical process

steps.action: They retain, as a suggestion, the mechanism of source events driving plate normal modes via free oscillations, which then produce compressive normal stress that releases delayed triggered events.
steps.quote: We suggest that the original source events (M ≥ M6.0) drive the normal mode responses of the individual plates via free oscillations

steps.action: They keep the local susceptibility method and the onset magnitude as an empirical proxy for a variable Mc in hazard analyses.
steps.quote: A method for analyzing a local region’s susceptibility to remote triggering is presented.

end.claim: Using ±2.85 degree regional boxes, 86% of global plate boundaries show susceptibility to remote triggering of high-magnitude earthquakes (19% with p<0.05) and 14% show none, each with a local onset magnitude.

decisive_move.sentence: Without the new local p-value curve method (minimum mid p-value over a rising lower magnitude bound, giving susceptibility and onset magnitude), neither the global maps nor the later mechanism tests would exist.

gates.evidence: Action: the data are an existing USGS/CMT catalog analysed retrospectively (§3 ¶1, 'retrospective analysis'); no hypothesis directed acquisition. Claim: the susceptibility p-values face a binomial null, and the Fig. 5 projections and the stress matchup face synthetic randomized catalogs that could have matched them (§2 ¶5, §2.1 ¶6); the mechanism has no rival and only one mode (24) of one plate is tested. Registration: the 72 h window, M5.0/M6.0 thresholds and approach were carried over from the 2018 paper, where the 3-day window 'gave the strongest global results' (§1.1 ¶1) on overlapping catalog data, so nothing was fixed before these data were seen. Mode 24 and the Fig. 5 binning were chosen without a stated prior rule.

imports.item: Binomial test with mid p-value (Lancaster 1961), framed by a coin-toss analogy
Finite element modal analysis in Abaqus (Dassault Systèmes SIMULIA)
Thin-plate resonance and normal modes driving stress changes
MATLAB binocdf and R pbinom for p-value calculation

novelty_claims.quote: The onset magnitude defined here is a new metric based on a regional analysis, and it delivers results based on data spanning 40 + years.
Here a method is developed to examine local earthquake history to determine how susceptible a given area is to remote triggering of high magnitude earthquakes.

limits: No review file was supplied, so no review sequence is coded. The Supplementary Information (Sections 1-3: baseline 0.501, synthetic catalogs, source-event distributions) was not supplied, so the design of the synthetic catalogs and the consistency check with the 2018 paper cannot be inspected. Sub-claim statuses: the onset magnitude versus p-value relation (Fig. 5) is regularity_in_range, holding for p-value bins 0.0-0.3 and extrapolated to p=1 beyond the data; the local method is capability_characterized only partly, with no synthetic-recovery test of the onset-magnitude estimator, and the onset algorithm is tuned to agree with visual inspection (§5.6 ¶1); the plate-resonance mechanism is at most a tentative best_explanation among no stated rivals ('We suggest'), tested on one plate (Cocos) and one mode (24) chosen from modes 4-30 with no stated selection rule (inference: the choice may be post hoc). The FEM omits the slab and uses a uniform thickness. Box size (±2.85 degrees), the 72 h window, the magnitude thresholds and the global baseline of 0.501 applied to all regions are not varied here. The 3-day window was the one that gave the strongest results in the earlier study on overlapping data (inference: a forking-path risk). The Discussion's 'We later suspected' (§3 ¶2) indicates that the mechanism search followed the Mc mismatch, an order different from the Results presentation; P is coded from that sentence. Composition: natures_repetition is a partial fit; the walk also has an exploratory pattern-then-hypothesis tail (Figs 6-8) that no composition captures.

disagreements.target: Boettcher and McGuire (2009), Mc of M6.4 for the Blanco Ridge
disagreements.support: The local onset magnitude for a box isolating Blanco Ridge transform faults is M5.1, while Gofar/Discovery segments agree with the published Mc values.
disagreements.quote: here the best example that isolates the transform faults of the Blanco Ridge yields an onset magnitude that is much lower (M5.1)

disagreements.target: Bird and Kagan (2004), generalized Mc estimates for seven tectonic settings
disagreements.support: Onset magnitudes are consistently lower than Bird and Kagan's Mc (e.g., M8.4 maximum versus M9.58 for subduction), reconciled by extrapolating Fig. 5 to p=1 and invoking a process that lowers Mc.
disagreements.quote: their estimates of MC are consistently greater than the onset magnitudes obtained here
